newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks, bonds fall; dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks, bonds fall; dollar mixed.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday, a day after the Dow Jones industrial average posted its second biggest point gain ever, while bonds slid on lack of follow-through buying after a strong Treasury note auction.
The dollar edged lower against most major currencies but rose against the pound as British polls showed next week's parliamentary elections could be much tighter than previously thought.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 20.87 points to 6,812.72. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,330 to 1,136 on moderately active volume of 489 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said investors turned cautious after propelling the Dow 173 points higher on Tuesday. But technology stocks gained as International Business Machines Corp., Intel Corp. and Microsoft Corp. also moved higher.

Earnings reports again dominated the session, with the big-name tech rally in particular linked to anticipation that IBM would release upbeat results. After the close, IBM reported flat earnings that were nevertheless better than most Wall Street analysts had expected.

"We're not setting the world on fire," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "It's a nervous kind of market and when people do come back in, they want to be in high-grade, liquid issues."
As has often been the case during the Dow's recent run, market breadth was fairly weak, with declining stocks outnumbering those that rose.
The 30-year Treasury fell a half point, or $5 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 7.08 percent from 7.04 percent at Tuesday's close. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Analysts said that once the flow of earnings reports ebbs, interest rate worries would likely once again grip the market.
"Next week, when the focus shifts from earnings, I think the market is going to go down," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers.

Shulman said he expected interest rates would soon be headed higher, with the 30-year bond yield rising to 7.50 percent. "That's not going to be friendly for stocks," he said. Long-term interest rates above 7 percent tend to draw money away stocks and into bonds.
In currency markets, the British pound fell to $1.6230 late Wednesday from $1.6333 late Tuesday. The dollar slid to 1.7135 German marks and 126.05 Japanese yen from 1.7172 marks and 126.32 yen.

Buoyed by gains in heating oil, crude oil for May delivery rose 14 cents a barrel to $19.73 at the New York Mercantile Exchange. May heating oil rose 0.82 cent higher at 55.65 cents a gallon after a sharp reduction in stockpiles was reported.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index rose 41.6 points to 4,387.7. Tokyo's Nikkei average rose 191.02 points to 18,735.47, its highest close in nearly two months.
